Animated movies have been giving children reasons to sleep with the lights on for generations. The Nightmare Before Christmas made a Christmas delivery genuinely threatening, while Coraline turned the promise of a better home into a particularly convincing nightmare. Their characters might look inviting on a poster, but watching the movies is another matter. A family-friendly rating doesn’t guarantee that everyone will leave feeling reassured.

That’s part of what makes those movies so satisfying to revisit in October. They take childhood fears seriously enough to build a story around them, even when the adults onscreen would prefer to dismiss the problem. Being small and having no one believe you is frightening before anything supernatural happens. Give those children a monster to deal with, and suddenly the adventure has considerably higher stakes than getting grounded.

Monster House is finding a Halloween audience on Peacock twenty years after its 2006 release. According to a U.S. movie chart, the animated horror comedy sits at No. 3, directly behind Coraline. It ranks above Trolls Band Together and How the Grinch Stole Christmas, with Casper also appearing in the top ten. That gives Peacock two unsettling animated adventures in its top three, making this a particularly good month for movies that taught their youngest viewers to be suspicious of perfectly ordinary homes.

‘Monster House’ Makes the Creepy Neighbor the Least of the Kids’ Problems
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/monster-house.jpeg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The Monster House roaring in 'Monster House'

blocks.x: Image via Columbia Pictures

Directed by Gil Kenan, the movie follows D.J., a boy keeping an eye on the intimidating house across the street. Its owner, Horace Nebbercracker, already gives the neighborhood children plenty of reasons to keep their distance. When D.J. discovers that the building itself is alive, he teams up with Chowder and Jenny to investigate. Mitchel Musso, Sam Lerner, and Spencer Locke voice the children, while Steve Buscemi plays Nebbercracker.

The premise takes a familiar childhood warning and gives it teeth. Staying off someone’s lawn becomes a matter of survival, and the house makes crossing the street look like a very poor decision. There’s comedy in the children’s arguments and questionable plans, but it never makes the threat feel harmless. The movie commits to making its monster scary, which is exactly what gives the adventure something worth overcoming.

It also understands how much danger changes when the characters have limited options. D.J. and his friends can’t simply call someone who will immediately accept that a house is trying to eat people. They have to investigate a threat they barely understand while knowing that getting closer could make them its next victims. That puts viewers in the uncomfortable position of wanting answers and wanting the children to stay as far away as possible.
Monster House is available to stream on Peacock.
